headline: New chip could let earbuds work without a phone

sources.title: New kind of AI audio chip transforms earbuds into always-on 'intelligent' devices that run without a smartphone. How does it work? (Live Science)
Qualcomm launches AI earbud chip, glasses platforms and a health alliance (The Next Web)
Qualcomm's New Minuscule Sound Chip Fits Wi-Fi Lossless Audio in Your Ears (Gizmodo)

chunks.text: One of the world's biggest makers of phone chips has [[unveiled]] a new chip for earbuds. The company {{showed off}} the chip at its [[annual summit]] in Hawaii, held from September 21 to 24. It is designed to run apps and AI tools directly inside earbuds, glasses, and [[hearing devices]]. Today, most earbuds need a nearby phone for this kind of work. For many tasks, the new chip could {{do away with}} that need.

verbs.correct: To display something proudly to others
verbs.wrong: To arrive at an event as planned
verbs.why: A proud parent shows off a child's drawing to every visitor, and a car maker shows off its newest model at a big fair. The company showed off the new earbud chip at its annual summit in Hawaii, held from September 21 to 24.

verbs.wrong: To repeat a task from the start
verbs.why: Online tickets do away with long lines at the box office, and a dishwasher can do away with hours of washing by hand. The new chip could do away with the need to carry a phone for many earbud tasks.

chunks.text: The chip pairs a small AI [[processor]] with the parts that handle sound. It has twice the AI power of the company's [[previous]] earbud chip. It also uses up to 40 percent less energy. [[Built-in]] wireless internet lets earbuds {{tap into}} [[cloud services]] without a phone. Users can make spoken requests, and an AI model can {{carry out}} tasks such as adding [[calendar entries]] or making [[online purchases]].

verbs.correct: To connect to and use something useful
verbs.wrong: To keep working hard at something
verbs.why: Students can tap into free online courses, and small shops tap into big online markets to find new buyers. Built-in wireless internet lets the earbuds tap into cloud services without going through a phone.

verbs.correct: To do a task that someone asks for
verbs.wrong: To keep doing something without stopping
verbs.why: A good assistant carries out the boss's requests quickly, and a robot vacuum carries out a cleaning schedule every morning. Users can speak a request, and an AI model can carry out tasks such as adding calendar entries or making online purchases.

chunks.text: [[Improved]] microphones {{pick up}} the wearer's voice more clearly. Better [[noise cancellation]] helps {{block out}} [[background sound]]. The chip can also translate speech [[in real time]]. Some future earbuds may even have tiny cameras that help the AI {{figure out}} what is around the wearer. The system would watch the wearer's [[surroundings]] to {{build up}} a [[personal profile]]. The company says the cameras would be [[low resolution]] and would use AI to hide the [[identities]] of people nearby.

verbs.correct: To detect a sound or signal
verbs.wrong: To choose one from a larger group
verbs.why: A baby monitor picks up the smallest cry, and a good radio picks up stations from far away. The chip works with improved microphones that pick up the wearer's voice more clearly.

verbs.correct: To stop a sound from being heard
verbs.wrong: To close an area so no one can enter
verbs.why: Thick walls block out the noise of the street, and good headphones block out the hum of a plane engine. Better noise cancellation on the chip helps block out background sound.

verbs.correct: To understand something by thinking about it
verbs.wrong: To include something when adding up a total
verbs.why: A new student figures out the bus routes after a few days, and a mechanic figures out why the engine makes a strange sound. Tiny cameras in future earbuds could help the AI figure out what is around the wearer.

verbs.correct: To create something little by little
verbs.wrong: To place a part inside a device
verbs.why: A new store builds up a list of loyal customers over the years, and a student builds up a strong vocabulary by reading every day. The system would watch the wearer's surroundings to build up a personal profile.

chunks.text: The head of the company's wearables business said interactions with AI "won't always happen through a screen." "They will happen through natural conversations," he added. The company cites its own research showing that up to 70 percent of users want more AI in their [[wearable devices]]. It is {{teaming up with}} several device makers, but no [[launch date]] has been set. One tech site said it is unclear whether the camera earbuds will ever {{come out}} as real products.

verbs.wrong: To support one person in an argument
verbs.why: A small bakery teams up with a local coffee shop for a weekend event, and a school teams up with a hospital to teach first aid. The company is teaming up with several device makers to build products with the new chip.

verbs.correct: To become available for people to buy
verbs.wrong: To happen without anyone planning it
verbs.why: A new video game comes out every fall, and a popular phone comes out in a new color each year. One tech site said it is unclear whether the camera earbuds will ever come out as real products.

mainIdea.s: A big chipmaker has shown a chip that lets earbuds and glasses run apps and AI by themselves. Built-in wireless internet means people could talk to AI tools without carrying a phone.
mainIdea.why: The chip has its own AI processor and internet connection, so earbuds can tap into cloud services and carry out spoken requests with no phone nearby.

mainIdea.s: A major chip company revealed an earbud chip that runs AI tools and apps without a phone. Its partners have already set a date, and the first camera earbuds go on sale next month.
mainIdea.why: Close, but no launch date has been set. One tech site said it is unclear whether the camera earbuds will ever come out as real products.

mainIdea.s: A phone maker has recalled thousands of wireless earbuds after reports that their batteries got too hot. Owners are being told to stop charging them and return them to stores.
mainIdea.why: There was no recall and no battery problem. A chipmaker showed off a new chip that lets earbuds run apps and AI without a phone.

lines.text: Did you hear that one of the big chipmakers {{showed off}} a new chip for earbuds?
A chip for earbuds? That doesn't sound like big news.
This one runs apps and AI right inside the earbuds. They wouldn't need your phone.
[[I'm all ears]]. How does it work, [[in plain English]]?
It has built-in wireless internet, so the earbuds can {{tap into}} cloud services on their own.
So earbuds could {{do away with}} the need for a phone?
For a lot of things, yes. You say what you want, and an AI model can {{carry out}} the task, like adding a calendar entry.
If it all works, I could leave my phone at home when I go for a run.
[[That's a big if]]. But the microphones {{pick up}} your voice better, and the noise cancellation can {{block out}} background sound.
Some earbuds might even have tiny cameras to help the AI {{figure out}} what's around you.
Cameras in my ears? I'm not sure how I feel about that.
Yeah, and it would {{build up}} a personal profile from what it sees. [[To be fair]], the company says the cameras would hide the identities of people nearby.
Okay, that helps a little. When can I buy a pair?
The company is {{teaming up with}} several device makers, but there's no launch date yet.
So the camera earbuds might never {{come out}} at all?
Maybe. One tech site said it's unclear.
Then [[I'll believe it when I see it]].

expressions.def: Used to say you are ready and eager to listen to what someone will tell you
ex: You found a cheaper flight? I'm all ears.
Tell me your plan for the weekend. I'm all ears.

expressions.def: Used to ask for something to be explained in simple words, without technical language
ex: The doctor used a lot of big words. What does it mean in plain English?
Can you explain the contract in plain English?

expressions.def: Used to say that something you just mentioned may well not happen
ex: We'll finish early if the weather holds. That's a big if.
He could win if he trains every day, but that's a big if.

expressions.def: Used to add a point that makes a criticism seem less strong
ex: The food was slow. To be fair, the place was very busy.
He missed the meeting. To be fair, nobody told him the time.

expressions.expr: I'll believe it when I see it
expressions.def: Used to say you doubt something will happen until you have proof
ex: They say the new bridge will open in May. I'll believe it when I see it.
My brother says he'll start running every morning. I'll believe it when I see it.
